lead: A cloud region is a set of data centres in one geographic area. Each data centre is a building full of racks, switches, power and cooling. A user reaches it through a chain: phone to local ISP, then transit or peering, then an internet exchange, then long fibre into the region. That physical path sets latency, the time a signal takes, and availability, whether the path and the building stay up. Bandwidth, the bits per second, is a different number. This chapter follows one request into a Mumbai region and then inside to a server rack.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for cloud regions and deployment models, and Chapter 2.5 for how traffic is spread once it reaches a region.

sections.h3: From the phone to the region

blocks.text: The user's phone joins an access network. The last mile is the final link from a street cabinet or radio tower to the user; it can be fibre, coax or mobile radio. The local ISP (internet service provider) owns that access network and sells the connection.

ISPs form a hierarchy. A tier 3 ISP is close to users and buys transit from larger providers. A tier 2 ISP covers a region or country and buys some transit. A tier 1 ISP owns a backbone that reaches many countries and usually buys no transit; it swaps traffic with other tier 1 ISPs. Transit is paid carriage: a customer pays a provider to carry its packets to the rest of the internet. Peering is a direct exchange between two networks, often without payment because both gain.

An internet exchange point (IXP) is a building or switch fabric where many ISPs meet to peer. It shortens paths: two networks at the same IXP exchange traffic without crossing a distant transit provider.

Latency is the time for a signal to cross the path, in milliseconds (ms). Bandwidth is capacity, in bits per second. A 1 Gbps link and a 10 Mbps link on the same fibre have the same travel time. Round-trip time (RTT) is the time to go there and back.

Some syllabi call this the public cloud infrastructure layer. A data centre is a building engineered for continuous operation. Servers sit in racks, metal frames roughly 2 m tall. Each rack has a top-of-rack (ToR) switch. Servers connect to the ToR by short copper or fibre links. ToR switches connect upward to aggregation switches, and aggregation switches connect to core switches. The core connects the building to long-haul fibre and to other data centres.

Power enters through transformers, switchgear, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and power distribution units (PDUs). A UPS carries the load for minutes until generators start. Cooling removes heat because servers turn almost all electrical energy into heat. PUE (power usage effectiveness) is total facility power divided by IT power. IT power is the power drawn by servers, storage and network gear. Total facility power adds cooling, losses and lighting. A PUE of 1.4 means every 1 W of IT needs 1.4 W at the building meter. Lower is better.

blocks.where: PUE is power usage effectiveness (no unit); P_total is total facility power in W or MW; P_IT is power drawn by IT equipment in the same unit.

blocks.text: Redundancy is described against N, the capacity needed. N+1 has one spare unit, such as one extra UPS or chiller. 2N has two full independent sets, so one set can fail or be maintained while the other carries all load. 2N costs more and uses more space.

A region is a geographic area with one or more data centres. An availability zone (AZ) is an isolated data centre or group of data centres inside a region, with independent power, cooling and network. A region with three AZs can lose one AZ and keep serving. Replicas are placed across AZs; Chapter 2.5 covers the failover.

Distance sets latency, not bandwidth alone. Light in glass travels at about 2×10⁸ m/s, two-thirds of its speed in vacuum. Route length is longer than map distance, so a measured RTT is a better guide than kilometres. A Chennai user talking to a Mumbai region often sees tens of milliseconds, while a farther region adds more.
Bandwidth matters for bulk transfer. A 1 MB page is 8 megabits. At 100 Mbps it takes 80 ms just to serialise, while fibre travel over 1,200 km is 6 ms one way. Both appear in the user's wait.

Availability comes from redundant paths and redundant building systems. One ISP is one failure. A cloud provider peers at IXPs and buys transit from several providers, so one backbone failure does not isolate a region. Inside, N+1 or 2N power and multiple AZs support the availability figure.

figure.caption: Every hop adds its own delay: 5 ms of access, 2 ms of ISP hops, 6 ms of fibre over 1,200 km and 0.5 ms of switching give 13.5 ms one way, so the round trip is 27 ms. The 6 ms fibre hop is fixed by distance, while the rack's draw of 1.5 MW of IT at PUE 1.4 is a separate number: 2.1 MW at the meter.

spec.title: One request, Chennai to Mumbai
spec.aria: A Chennai phone reaches its local ISP in 5 ms, ISP hops take 2 ms, 1,200 km of fibre into the Mumbai region takes 6 ms and data centre switching takes 0.5 ms, giving 13.5 ms one way and 27 ms round trip; the top-of-rack switch feeds a server rack drawing 1.5 MW of IT at PUE 1.4, which is 2.1 MW at the meter.

examples.question: A Chennai user talks to a Mumbai region 1,200 km away over fibre at 2×10⁸ m/s. The access network adds 5 ms, ISP hops add 2 ms, and data centre switching adds 0.5 ms. Find the one-way delay and the round-trip time. The data centre draws 1.5 MW for IT equipment at PUE 1.4 and pays ₹8 per kWh. Find its monthly energy cost for 730 hours.
steps: One-way delay = 6 ms + 5 ms + 2 ms + 0.5 ms = 13.5 ms.
IT power = 1.5 MW. Total facility power = 1.5 MW × 1.4 = 2.1 MW.
Monthly energy = 2.1 MW × 730 h = 1,533 MWh = 1,533,000 kWh.
examples.answer: The one-way delay is 13.5 ms, the RTT is 27 ms, the facility draws 2.1 MW, monthly energy is 1,533 MWh (1,533,000 kWh), and the monthly energy cost is ₹1,22,64,000, about ₹1.23 crore.
examples.check:
distance_m = 1200000
speed_m_s = 2e8
access_ms = 5
isp_ms = 2
dc_ms = 0.5
fibre_ms = distance_m / speed_m_s * 1000
one_way_ms = fibre_ms + access_ms + isp_ms + dc_ms
rtt_ms = 2 * one_way_ms
it_mw = 1.5
pue = 1.4
total_mw = it_mw * pue
hours = 730
energy_mwh = total_mw * hours
energy_kwh = energy_mwh * 1000
rate = 8
cost = energy_kwh * rate
print(one_way_ms)
print(rtt_ms)
print(total_mw)
print(energy_mwh)
print(energy_kwh)
print(cost)

traps: Bandwidth is not latency: a fat link can still be far away. A 1 Gbps link does not shorten the 6 ms fibre hop.
PUE is total facility power ÷ IT power. Inverting it gives 0.71 for PUE 1.4, which is wrong.
Use one-way distance for one-way delay and double it for RTT. Do not double the distance and also double the time.
An IXP is a meeting point, not an ISP. A tier 1 ISP is not the same as a top-of-rack switch.
N+1 is one spare unit; 2N is a full duplicate. They are not the same cost or floor space.

quiz.q: What is an IXP, and what does it save?
quiz.a: An internet exchange point is a shared switch fabric where ISPs peer. It saves transit distance and often transit cost by keeping traffic local.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between transit and peering.
quiz.a: Transit is paid carriage by a provider to reach the rest of the internet. Peering is a direct traffic exchange between two networks, often settlement-free, where each reaches the other's customers.

quiz.q: A fibre route is 900 km at 2×10⁸ m/s. Access adds 4 ms, ISP hops add 3 ms, and data centre switching adds 0.5 ms. Find one-way delay and RTT.
Why does upgrading a user from 10 Mbps to 100 Mbps not remove the 30 ms RTT to a distant region?
quiz.a: Bandwidth changes serialisation time, not propagation delay. The signal still travels the same fibre length at about 2×10⁸ m/s, so RTT stays near 30 ms; only bulk transfer time falls.

quiz.q: A data centre draws 800 kW for IT at PUE 1.5 and pays ₹7 per kWh for 730 h. Find total facility power, monthly energy in kWh, and cost.
A region has three AZs. Explain why the provider may still advertise less than 100% availability for a single VM in one AZ.
quiz.a: An AZ isolates power, cooling and network, but a single VM has no replica in another AZ. Hardware failure or maintenance in that AZ can stop the VM, so the single-VM availability is lower than the multi-AZ service availability.

quiz.q: What is the last mile, and why does it often dominate user latency?
quiz.a: The last mile is the final link from the local network to the user, often radio or old copper. It adds access delays and can be congested, so it can dominate over a long, fast backbone.
PUE = total facility power ÷ IT power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Network engineers use anycast to send users to the nearest healthy region, and DDoS scrubbing centres absorb attack traffic before it reaches a region. Newer curricula discuss liquid cooling and waste-heat reuse to lower PUE below 1.2. Search for 'internet exchange point', 'cloud region availability zone' and 'PUE data centre' to go further.
